title: NetMamba+ in 30 minutes
subtitle: Read the evidence. Explain the system.
mission: Explain the tested model, its results and its limits.
orientation: Read, answer, then review. Finish with a two-minute explanation. Setup and optional references are outside the planned 30 minutes; your pace may vary.

walkthrough.label: Every file and every release attachment

teaching.text: A packet is one small network message. A flow groups related packets into a conversation. An intrusion detection system (IDS) observes traffic and raises alerts. A classifier assigns categories; capture, alert rules and blocking require additional components.
The NetMamba+ paper combines bytes, packet sizes and time gaps: three views, or modalities. Mamba processes a sequence by updating a numerical state. The earlier NetMamba used bytes alone.

This repository records a reproduction attempt on an NVIDIA GB10 GPU: native builds, short pretraining, three full fine-tuning runs and saved-model inference worked. A GPU accelerates many numerical operations in parallel.

options: A tested flow classifier and recorded replay
questions.explanation: Classification works. Capture and operational alert handling remain future work.

segments.title: Three files, two different kinds of data

teaching.text: The supplied PDF describes the research, not a ready-to-use dataset. The supplied CICIDS2017 CSV contains {{cic_rows}} packet rows and 15 labels. The UNSW CSV contains {{unsw_rows}} packet rows and 10 labels. Each has 1,500 payload-byte columns plus TTL (remaining network hops), total length, protocol, time delta and label.

Neither CSV establishes connection identity and ordering. Adjacent rows cannot be assumed to form one conversation. The CICIDS2017 scan also found negative time deltas, with timing units unestablished. UNSW is a separate packet export, not a second native flow split. These were metadata profiles, not training runs or exhaustive payload validation. Training directly on them would create a packet-classifier adaptation.

For the original model, we acquired the authors’ processed CICIoT2022 flow release. CICIoT2022 and CICIDS2017 are different datasets. There are {{train_rows}} training, {{valid_rows}} validation and {{test_rows}} test flows. Training examples teach weights; validation chooses a checkpoint; the test split measures that selected model.

rows: Known category / meaning of each class index

teaching.text: The six class indices mean 0 Flood, 1 RTSP Brute Force, 2 Audio, 3 Other, 4 Cameras and 5 Home Automation. The last four are IoT device/power categories. A compatible JSON file must preserve the native structure and preprocessing assumptions; similar column names are insufficient. IoT means Internet of Things: connected cameras and home devices. Flood overwhelms with traffic; RTSP brute force repeatedly tries access to a streaming protocol.

questions.prompt: You receive five neighboring CSV rows. Can you pass them as one native flow?
options: Yes; five rows satisfy the packet count
No; relatedness and order are unestablished
questions.explanation: The model requires one established flow with byte, size and gap sequences. Arbitrary grouping changes the experiment. Use the compatible release or establish a validated extractor.

segments.title: How the model learns and predicts

teaching.text: The original loader takes five packets, each with up to 320 stored bytes: 1,600 values. The paper’s packet layout is 80 header bytes plus 240 payload bytes. Released flows already contain this extraction; our wrapper does not reconstruct headers from the uploaded CSVs. Bytes are scaled to [-1, 1]. The loader also pads or truncates the first 20 sizes and 20 gaps.

Sizes are clipped to 0–1,500; the size padding value 1,501 is clipped to 1,500. A finite nonnegative gap x becomes (1+x)/(2+x); padding infinity maps to 1. For classification, four-byte groups yield 400 byte tokens. Add 20 size tokens, 20 gap tokens and three summary tokens: 443. Four Mamba blocks process them; the three summary vectors are added before classification. Internal state belongs to this input computation, not an implemented live connection cache.

rows: Unlabeled flow features → reconstruct masked features → learned encoder
Flows plus labels → update encoder/classifier weights → six-class checkpoint
Flow features plus frozen checkpoint → forward calculation → six logits and a selected class

teaching.text: Pretraining hides 90% of byte strides and 15% each of sizes and intervals in the source preset. A loss measures training error; the optimizer changes weights to reduce it. An epoch passes through the training loader. Our short pretraining check completed 132 updates. The three full fine-tuning runs instead began from the authors’ released pretrained checkpoint. They did not use that short-check checkpoint.

Logits are raw outputs. Softmax normalizes them into display scores. Labeled evaluation compares predictions with known answers to compute accuracy. Unlabeled prediction has no known answers and therefore cannot report accuracy. A successful manifest or export provenance binds the checkpoint to its class meanings; six output numbers alone do not identify those meanings.

questions.prompt: At inference, which action is correct?
options: Freeze weights, use flow features, preserve the class mapping
questions.explanation: Fine-tuning updates weights. Validation selects the checkpoint. Inference freezes it; known test labels are used afterward for scoring, not model selection or prediction inputs.

segments.title: What we changed, and where it lives

teaching.text: The authors’ repository provides the model, tensor loader and training engines. Our repository fetches that code at commit {{source_commit}} and checks source identity. The model and loader remain unchanged. For GB10/CUDA 13, disposable native-extension build copies receive architecture/compiler compatibility edits. This is a compatibility port, not proof of an identical paper environment.

rows: Pinned experiment recipe, asset identities and runtime dependencies
Validate source/data; launch original training; save run manifests
Labeled scoring / unlabeled inference / recorded browser output
Build, measure, publish and test important failure behavior
Actual logs, hashes and predictions behind claims
Curated research and council records; not a raw private chat dump

teaching.text: A manifest is a lab notebook for one run. A SHA-256 hash identifies file bytes; it does not prove scientific validity. Downloaded data, upstream source and trained weights stay local. The complete repository walkthrough explains every tracked file and release download; use it after this timed overview.

options: We replaced the authors’ neural model with a new implementation
We wrapped pinned original code and ported native builds for GB10
questions.explanation: The wrapper adds validation, provenance, inference, measurement and teaching tools. Native compiler compatibility edits do not establish an exact reproduction of the paper’s hardware or protocol.

segments.title: What actually ran, and what the numbers mean

teaching.text: All three declared seeds completed {{epochs}} fine-tuning epochs and {{updates}} updates each. A seed controls random choices; the three seeds used the same dataset split. Checkpoints were selected by validation accuracy, then strictly reloaded for test inference. All three results were retained.

The sample standard deviation is {{accuracy_sd}} percentage points, not a confidence interval. Accuracy is the fraction correct. F1 balances precision and recall; macro F1 treats classes equally, while weighted F1 weights their support. A confusion matrix exposes which true categories were confused with which predictions.

Source-based training used batch 128 and an effective learning rate of 0.001 on GB10; the paper describes batch 64, rate 0.002 and A100 hardware. The released checkpoint’s full pretraining history is unknown. Short reconstruction pretraining worked, but the paper’s full 150,000-step pretraining was not repeated. The cause of the accuracy gap has not been isolated.

Five raw-input overlaps were found between training/validation and six between training/test. Physical independence and original pretraining exposure remain unestablished. Rechecking the same test set demonstrates repeatability, not independent validation. GPU numerical checks and saved-model agreement support execution correctness, not operational detection accuracy.

questions.prompt: Which sentence belongs in the customer meeting?
options: Three runs averaged {{mean_accuracy}} on the released split; exact paper reproduction remains open
questions.explanation: Keep all seeds and the comparison conditions. The best run is useful for the preselected demo but is not the three-run mean. Neither repeated test evaluation nor a sample standard deviation establishes generalization to customer traffic.

teaching.text: This is recorded GPU output from seed 0, not live browser inference. The full saved replay has {{test_rows}} flows: 950 correct and 91 incorrect. Its 402 attack-category predictions are not 402 verified operational alerts. Changing replay speed changes display timing only.

Read the saved row below. First identify the predicted category and its score; then reveal the dataset’s known label. The example was deliberately selected to examine a mistake, not estimate its frequency. Softmax can be confidently wrong. One row cannot establish a false-positive rate or a calibrated probability of attack.

questions.prompt: How should an analyst describe this row after revealing its label?
options: The {{demo_score}} score proves an RTSP attack
It predicts RTSP Brute Force but disagrees with the dataset’s Other label
A high score makes ground truth unnecessary
questions.explanation: Row 635 is a recorded error: predicted class 1 versus labeled class 3. The score ranks these six classes; it is not a verified attack probability. An operational alert would need an independently validated policy and investigation.

segments.title: Set it up, use it and check it

rows: Open this HTML, the recorded replay, PDF or PowerPoint; no account/GPU needed
Python 3.10+; clone the repository or extract the audited package
Follow the tested GB10/CUDA runbook; separately fetch pinned source, data and original weights

teaching.text: For the current repository, the CPU commands below run harness/course tests and check saved evidence. Expect OK and verifier status passed. The audited release’s 54 tests are historical; current main adds course tests. These checks do not rerun GPU training. A failure is a finding to inspect, not a reason to blindly regenerate hashes.

python3 -m unittest discover -s tests -v
python3 tools/verify_package.py
python3 tools/verify_course.py

The GPU route acquires assets, validates flows, builds two custom extensions, checks numerical operations, trains, then evaluates or predicts. Use a fresh output directory for each run and retain checkpoint provenance. predict.py accepts assembled native flow JSON, not either supplied CSV. GPU setup and execution are follow-up work outside these 30 minutes.

The audited release offers the complete ZIP, briefing PDF, slide PDF, editable PPTX, SHA256SUMS-release.txt, release-inventory.json and release-verification.json. The inventory names files; checksums identify bytes; the receipt records tested downloads. The ZIP contains documents, code and evidence, not raw data or weights. This newer course is a separate HTML download and is not inside that historical ZIP.

Two independent native builds passed seven numerical checks each. Strict evaluations matched the saved metrics for all seeds. A full seed-0 unlabeled recheck matched all 1,041 predicted classes and logits in that run. Linux was tested; a successful CPU check does not establish universal Windows, CPU-model or NPU support.

questions.prompt: A colleague has a laptop and wants to verify the reported scores. Which route is appropriate?
options: Use Python CPU tests and the package verifier; inspect the saved evidence
Treat opening the PPTX as a new model evaluation
Begin by converting five CSV rows into a flow
questions.explanation: The verifier recomputes metrics from saved predictions and checks identities. Fresh predictions need the GPU setup and a provenance-bound classifier. If hashes disagree, preserve the failure and obtain a coherent package or review the intentional change.

segments.title: From classifier to IDS and accelerator

teaching.text: A live IDS would need capture → connection grouping → compatible tensors → inference → calibrated alert policy → analyst review. The source extractor has hardcoded paths and a missing helper; a compatible live pipeline has not been established.

A SmartNIC or DPU could steer packets and prepare flows. A GPU or supported neural processing unit (NPU) could classify them. This is a proposed division of work. Eager GPU inference works, but tested Torch graph capture failed at a custom causal-convolution operator. Saving model-only weights did not solve graph export. No NPU compiler or SmartNIC deployment was tested.

The model-only batch-one median was about 0.88 ms, excluding capture, flow waiting, preprocessing and transfers. It is not end-to-end IDS latency. The paper’s online throughput example concerns byte-only NetMamba. Next work includes independent traffic, extraction compatibility, alert calibration, export/operator support and inherited data/code rights.

options: NPU support and live latency remain untested
questions.explanation: GPU execution does not establish NPU export or live IDS behavior.

activity.instruction: Speak for two minutes without reading. Use the remaining minute to check this rubric and correct one weak claim. Ask a colleague to score it if available.
rubric: Explain flows, the three inputs, training and frozen inference.
State all three runs’ mean, and distinguish the paper result.
Explain what the recorded demo proves and its error.
Name the working checks and where their evidence lives.
Separate future IDS/NPU work from tested execution.
activity.closing: A useful explanation meets all five points with no inflated claims. This is self-assessment, not independent certification.
